claim_verdicts.evidence: Grepped verbatim in the local mirror. RFC 9112 §3: "A request-line begins with a method token, followed by a single space (SP), the request-target, and another single space (SP), and ends with the protocol version." RFC 9110 §9.1: "The request method token is the primary source of request semantics; it indicates the purpose for which the client has made this request and what is expected by the client as a successful result." Both halves of the claim (position, and naming the intended action) are covered.

RFC 9110 §9.2.1: "This definition of safe methods does not prevent an implementation from including behavior that is potentially harmful, that is not entirely read-only, or that causes side effects while invoking a safe method." And, on the owner: "If the purpose of such a resource is to perform an unsafe action, then the resource owner MUST disable or disallow that action when it is accessed using a safe request method." A MUST addressed to the resource owner, with no enforcement mechanism — exactly what the claim says.

RFC 9110 §9.3.1: "The GET method requests transfer of a current selected representation for the target resource." §9.2.1: "Request methods are considered 'safe' if their defined semantics are essentially read-only; i.e., the client does not request, and does not expect, any state change on the origin server as a result of applying a safe method to a target resource", and "Of the request methods defined by this specification, the GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE methods are defined to be safe."

RFC 9110 §9.3.3: "The POST method requests that the target resource process the representation enclosed in the request according to the resource's own specific semantics." Among the listed functions: "Creating a new resource that has yet to be identified by the origin server". The claim's hedge "commonly" is right — creation is one of four listed uses, not the definition.

RFC 9110 §9.3.4: "The PUT method requests that the state of the target resource be created or replaced with the state defined by the representation enclosed in the request message content." Also §9.3.4: "the enclosed representation in a PUT request is defined as replacing the state of the target resource. Hence, the intent of PUT is idempotent and visible to intermediaries." The claim restates the first sentence without adding anything.

PATCH is not defined by RFC 9110, the only HTTP source in content/versions.yaml; RFC 5789 is neither a docs root there nor mirrored (refs/rfc holds 6265, 9110, 9111, 9112). RFC 9110 §14.5 still states the substance: "Partial resource updates are also possible by targeting a separately identified resource ... or by using a different method that has been specifically defined for partial updates (for example, the PATCH method defined in [RFC5789])." Nothing in the mirror suggests PATCH replaces a resource whole.

RFC 9110 §9.3.5: "The DELETE method requests that the origin server remove the association between the target resource and its current functionality. In effect, this method is similar to the 'rm' command in UNIX: it expresses a deletion operation on the URI mapping of the origin server." The claim is a near-verbatim restatement of the first sentence.

RFC 9110 §9.2.2, opening sentence: "A request method is considered 'idempotent' if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request." The claim reproduces it, keeping "intended", and §3 of the lesson keeps that word too ("the same intended effect on the server — the same stored orders —").

RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent." §9.2.1: "the GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE methods are defined to be safe." POST is defined by this specification and is absent from that list; PATCH is not defined by RFC 9110 at all, only referenced as "the PATCH method defined in [RFC5789]", so "not on that list" is precise and asserts nothing more about PATCH.

RFC 9110 §9.2.2 settles both halves: "It knows that repeating the request will have the same intended effect, even if the original request succeeded, though the response might differ." And: "the idempotent property only applies to what has been requested by the user; a server is free to log each request separately, retain a revision control history, or implement other non-idempotent side effects for each idempotent request."

No permitted source covers form-resubmission confirmation: content/versions.yaml has no HTML or browser key, refs/ has no browser mirror, and no browser can be run here. The nearest text in the mirror is RFC 9110 §9.2.1: "A user agent SHOULD distinguish between safe and unsafe methods when presenting potential actions to a user" — about presenting actions, not about reloads. Kind is behavior, so this does not block; but see the §6 issue, where the lesson drops the hedge.

RFC 9110 §9.3.1: "The response to a GET request is cacheable; a cache MAY use it to satisfy subsequent GET and HEAD requests unless otherwise indicated by the Cache-Control header field." §9.3.5: "Responses to the DELETE method are not cacheable. If a successful DELETE request passes through a cache that has one or more stored responses for the target URI, those stored responses will be invalidated." The lesson's "never of a DELETE answer" is therefore accurate, not overstated.

RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "Idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response." And: "A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent ... or some means to detect that the original request was never applied." The claim as written matches; the lesson sentence built on it does not — see the §4 issue.

RFC 9110 §15.3.2: "The 201 (Created) status code indicates that the request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created. The primary resource created by the request is identified by either a Location header field in the response or, if no Location header field is received, by the target URI" — matching the claim's condition "when that field is present". §9.3.3 supports the lesson's "expected to send": the origin server "SHOULD send a 201 (Created) response containing a Location header field".

RFC 9110 §15.3.5: "The 204 (No Content) status code indicates that the server has successfully fulfilled the request and that there is no additional content to send in the response content." And, decisively: "A 204 response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers."

curl has no key in versions.yaml and no refs/ mirror, and no command could be run in this session, so this rests on the repo's own artefacts. methods.sh:9 carries -w 'GET    /api/v1/orders/1  -> %{http_code}\n' and captured line 1 is "GET    /api/v1/orders/1  -> 200": the label printed as typed, %{http_code} replaced, no body although @getOrder responds with JSON (-o /dev/null). The flagless line matched Caddyfile @getOrder (method GET); the -d line, carrying no -X, matched @postOrder (method POST) → 201 + Location. -sS is the only switch the artefacts do not settle.

Caddyfile header: "Caddy serves the Đơn Hàng static site and answers a few fixed API paths ... There is no application behind these answers yet; that arrives at stage-1." The order handlers are literal `respond` directives with constant bodies ({"id":13,...,"new"} 201, {"id":1,...,"paid"} 200, {"id":1,...,"shipped"} 200, "" 204), so no request can change what a later one sees. Read from the checked-out working tree, not from the tag object: git could not be run here (see the §5 code issue).

The committed capture is character-for-character the lesson's output block: the five "-> 200/201/200/200/204" lines, then "HTTP/1.1 201 Created" and "Location: /api/v1/orders/13", then {"id":1,"customer_id":1,"status":"paid"} twice. Each code traces to a Caddyfile handler: PUT and PATCH share @replaceOrder (both 200), @postOrder sets header Location "/api/v1/orders/13" and responds 201, @deleteOrder responds "" 204.

The conditional form is carried by claims 12 and 13, both verified from the mirror: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 "a cache MAY use it to satisfy subsequent GET and HEAD requests", §9.3.5 "Responses to the DELETE method are not cacheable", §9.2.2 "A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests." Machines on the path do read the method and act differently on it, which is what the claim asserts under its stated condition.

issues.text: Stated as fact about client libraries, and RFC 9110 §9.2.2 documents the opposite happening: "Some clients take a riskier approach and attempt to guess when an automatic retry is possible. For example, a client might automatically retry a POST request if the underlying transport connection closed before any part of a response is received." The spec's rule is a SHOULD NOT on the client, not a description of what libraries do. A reader is left believing a POST can never be sent twice by itself — the belief backend.l2.idempotent-endpoints exists to break.
issues.fix: Turn the description into the rule plus the exception: "...and should not retry a POST unless the person who wrote the call said that this one request is safe to send twice, because it cannot know whether the first arrived — though some libraries retry it anyway when the connection closed before any answer came back."
issues.quote: and will not retry a POST unless the person who wrote the call said that this one request is safe to send twice

issues.text: Unlisted claim, and it is the absolute form of claim 11, which is unverified: no browser or HTML source is permitted by content/versions.yaml and none exists under refs/. §4 and summary line 4 both hedge the same statement with "usually"; this bullet drops the hedge and asserts every reload. The strongest thing the mirror says is RFC 9110 §9.2.1, "A user agent SHOULD distinguish between safe and unsafe methods when presenting potential actions to a user" — a SHOULD about presenting actions, not a guarantee about reloads.
issues.fix: Match the hedge used elsewhere: "...and a reload usually asks the reader to confirm." Keep claim 11's wording ("usually asks") identical in §4, §6 and summary line 4.
issues.quote: and every reload asks the reader to confirm

issues.text: "here" reads as the whole block, and the block does more: the `-D -` line prints the status line and `Location`, and the last two `curl -sS "$base/1"` lines print the order body — both visible in the output block right below. Only the five `-w` lines print nothing but a label and a code. The next sentence, "they ... print the response headers", contradicts "nothing but". The same slip repeats in "The POST line is ... the only one carrying a body": the later POST carries `-d` too.
issues.fix: Scope both sentences to the first five lines: "Each of the five lines above prints nothing but its `-w` format string, with `%{http_code}` replaced by the status code that came back." and "Of those five, the POST line is the only one addressed to the list in `base` and the only one carrying a body."
issues.quote: What it prints here is nothing but the label typed into `-w` plus `%{http_code}`, the status code that came back.

issues.text: "That is why" points at the sentence before it, which is about PATCH. A browser sends an HTML form with GET or POST, never PATCH, so as written the lesson gives PATCH's uncertain repeatability as the reason for the reload prompt. Summary line 4 keeps the causality right ("POST is not idempotent, which is why a browser usually asks"); §4 does not.
issues.fix: Name the cause: "Because POST is not idempotent, a browser usually asks before sending a form again when you reload." Or move that sentence up so it follows "...ten POSTs to the list ask for ten new orders." and let the PATCH sentence close the paragraph.
issues.quote: PATCH is not on the list either: whether repeating it is harmless depends on the patch. That is why a browser usually asks before sending a form again when you reload.

issues.text: Code verification was partial in this session: git and tools/extract-code could not be executed (every git invocation was refused), so the block was compared against the checked-out working tree of examples/don-hang instead of the `stage-0` tag object. Lines 4-25 of scripts/http/methods.sh match the block character-for-character there, and the working tree sits on branch auto/stage-0 (refs/heads/auto/stage-0 = ff911b0) while refs/tags/stage-0 = 664d38a, which per the tag-object rule is not by itself a mismatch.
issues.fix: Before approval, re-run `tools/extract-code scripts/http/methods.sh --tag stage-0 --lines 4-25` in a session where git is available and confirm the block byte-for-byte; no change to the lesson text is implied.

issues.text: The keys (a, c, e) are right, but the stem's test is wrong: a repeated PUT or DELETE does make the server do work — RFC 9110 §9.2.2 says "a server is free to log each request separately, retain a revision control history, or implement other non-idempotent side effects for each idempotent request". What idempotency compares is the state left behind, which is what the explanation actually says ("leaves the server in the state one call would have left it").
issues.fix: Reword the stem in both languages: "Select all requests to the lab it may repeat this way without changing what the server ends up holding." / "Chọn tất cả request tới lab mà nó gửi lại được như vậy mà không làm đổi thứ server giữ lại sau cùng."
issues.quote: Select all requests to the lab it may repeat this way without asking the server for extra work.

issues.text: Every other method got a reason I could check: ten GETs, ten PUTs, ten DELETEs, ten POSTs. PATCH gets none. 'Depends on the patch' tells me the answer is somewhere in the body I send, but I cannot invent an example of a patch that is unsafe to repeat, so I finished the paragraph unable to decide whether a PATCH I write myself would be idempotent — which is exactly the judgement the sentence asks me to make.
issues.quote: PATCH is not on the list either: whether repeating it is harmless depends on the patch.
issues.fix: Extend that sentence with one contrast: '...depends on the patch: a patch that sets the status to paid leaves the same order after ten sends, while a patch that asks to add one more item does not.'

issues.text: 'That is why' asks me to connect a browser form to what I just read, but nothing in the lesson says which method a form is sent with. I know POST is not idempotent; I do not know that submitting a form sends a POST, so the reason lands on nothing and I had to take the sentence on trust. Summary line 4 repeats the same jump.
issues.quote: That is why a browser usually asks before sending a form again when you reload.
issues.fix: Put the missing link in the sentence: 'A form is usually sent with POST, which is why a browser usually asks before sending it again when you reload.'

issues.text: 'Verb' appears in the title and again in summary line 5 as if I already knew it means the method, but the body never says the two words are the same thing. Reading the summary I stopped to check whether a verb was a fourth thing beside method, address and body. The quiz explanations use it too.
issues.quote: a wrong verb misleads intermediaries that may reuse a GET answer
issues.fix: Tie the two words together once in §4: 'The word you kept changing in the situation is the HTTP method, also called the verb.'

issues.text: The stem says 'requests to the lab', and §5 told me that at this tag nothing is stored, so a second POST changes nothing there either — by the lesson's own words option b is safe at the lab and wrong only behind a real application. I could not decide between reading the stem literally (a, b, c, e) and reading it as being about a real server (a, c, e).
issues.quote: Select all requests to the lab it may repeat this way without asking the server for extra work.
issues.fix: Move the stem off the lab in both languages: 'A client library repeats a request by itself when a timeout leaves it without an answer. Behind a real application, select all requests it may repeat this way.' / '...Sau một ứng dụng thật, chọn tất cả request nó gửi lại được như vậy.'

issues.text: 'Tag stage-0' turns up in the first sentence and again in §5 and the Try it step, and I never learn what a tag of the example repository is. I guessed it names a version of the repo and that guess carried me through, but I was guessing from the first line of the lesson.
issues.quote: the lab site the example repository starts for you (tag `stage-0`)
issues.fix: Say it once, in that same parenthesis: '(at `stage-0`, the point in the example repository this lesson uses)'.

issues.text: The prose lists `Content-Type` among the plumbing without saying what it carries, and the value `application/json` plus the `{"customer_id":1}` body are never named as a format anywhere. I could ignore them here, but quiz q1 offers 'which format the client used for the body' as an option, so the exam expects a word the lesson never gives me.
issues.quote: set the `Content-Type` header, and print the response headers
issues.fix: Say what it carries where it is listed: 'set the `Content-Type` header, which tells the server what format the body is in, and print the response headers.'

issues.text: I read this as: PUT and PATCH really changed something. Two sentences later I learn the DELETE removed nothing because nothing is stored, and I had to go back and re-read the earlier sentence as 'reported' rather than 'changed'. The 200s are the same kind of pretend answer as the 204, and only the 204 gets that warning.
issues.quote: PUT and PATCH report that a change was accepted
issues.fix: Add two words: 'PUT and PATCH report that a change was accepted, though nothing here was changed'.

issues.text: `404` arrives with no explanation next to `204`, which the lesson does explain. I inferred from 'the rest find nothing' that it means there was nothing there, but I was inferring; the lesson that covers status codes is listed as a later one in Connections.
issues.quote: The first DELETE of an order can answer `204` and the second `404`
issues.fix: Gloss it in place: '...can answer `204` and the second `404` — nothing there to remove — yet both leave the order gone.'

issues.text: I read this three times. 'Is wrong' sounds like the client and the intermediary made a mistake, when what I think is meant is that they were misled by a server that broke the promise. The sentence is the pivot of the section's first idea, so the ambiguity costs more here than elsewhere.
issues.quote: and every client and intermediary that trusts the meaning is wrong
issues.fix: Replace the ending: '...and every client and intermediary that trusts the meaning is then misled.'

issues.text: Two long paragraphs in a row are switch bookkeeping — what `-w` prints, which lines carry `-X`, which one carries `-d`, which address each uses, what the last part prints. I had to re-read the second one to keep track of 'the four requests', 'the POST line', 'the last three' and 'the last part'. The point I needed (only the method differs) is the first clause and then it is buried.
issues.quote: Among the four requests to `base/1` only the method differs; the POST line changes the address as well.
issues.fix: Cut the second paragraph to what the reader must notice: keep 'Among the four requests to `base/1` only the method differs; the POST line changes the address as well and is the only one carrying a body', keep the `-X`/`-d` sentence, and drop the recap of the last part, which the output block already shows.

issues.text: Explanation b says the first call 'removes the row'. Nothing in the lesson has rows — orders are stored, and at this tag nothing is stored at all. I stopped to work out whether a row was a new thing I had missed.
issues.quote: The first call is indeed the one that removes the row
issues.fix: Use the lesson's word in both languages: 'The first call is indeed the one that removes the order'.

issues.text: Two explanations (q2 b and q4 b) call `/api/v1/orders` 'the collection', but the lesson always calls it the list or the list address. I had to stop and check that the collection was the same thing as the list rather than some other part of the address.
issues.quote: it is addressed to the collection and asks for what you sent to be processed there
issues.fix: Replace 'the collection' with 'the list address' in q2 explanation b and q4 explanation b, in both languages, matching §4's wording.
